catalog_quote: Each phonemic word of more than one syllable carries a single primary stress. 2.1 Stress There is a suprasegmental item of stress which is considered to be phonemic. Its occurrence in any word is unpredictable but it identifies a syllable on which it falls as being one of the last three syllables of a word. On many occasions the position of primary stress / / is the minimal difference between a pair of words, e.g. gayáŋ 'a type of spear'; gáyaŋ 'crow'; ʔirít 'outskirts, edge'; ʔírit 'eggs of head-lice'; bawí 'repent'; báwi 'field shelter'; bokár 'wild pig'; bókar 'disperse' ... Furthermore, there is a feature of stress which is considered to be non-phonemic since its occurrence can always be predicted in terms of primary stress. This feature is termed secondary stress. ... sweep_summary: Central Bontoc is in the catalog as lexical (Reid 1963, revised web copy: phonemic, unpredictable primary stress on one of the last three syllables). this search of works with stress in the title turned up a single title-keyword item, Thurgood 1997 'Bontok reduplication and prosodic templates' (Oceanic Linguistics 36(1):135-148, DOI 10.2307/3623073), already on our per-language bibliography and list of works to obtain. It is closed on JSTOR with no open copy anywhere checked (Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, HathiTrust, archive.org, author pages); only the OpenAlex abstract was obtained and ( updated). The abstract concerns heavy-syllable reduplication, gemination, metathesis and prosodic-template copying and is silent on stress placement, so the item is classed prosody-but-not-word-stress, not-read, low priority. No new first-hand stress statement was read; the catalog's deciding source (Reid 1963, held and previously verified verbatim, with Reid 2005 and Aoyama & Reid 2006 already held by the project) stands unchanged.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for cent2292 has an empty rule and no existing statements; this source supplies the first explicit statement: stress is contrastive/phonemic, hence lexical (unpredictable). It refers back to Reid (1963), 'Phonology of Central Bontoc', for the original description. Describes the Guinaang dialect of Central Bontok specifically (barangay Guinaang), matching the catalog entry.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) in Guinaang Central Bontok; it is listed as a phonemic element ('V́, Vowel stress') in both the 1960 and the 2004 phoneme inventories, so its position is not predictable from syllable count. The loanword tables show both final stress (biglá 'suddenly', sakbáy 'before', dakkél 'big', garúd 'so, then', adayó 'far') and penultimate stress (lában 'fight', grábe 'serious', ígid 'edge', túlong 'helper', dánon 'reach') on Bontok/Ilokano forms.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the paper's topic is segmental change under Ilokano/English contact, and stress is only characterised as contrastive, with no placement rule given
new_statements.identity_note: Reid 2005 and Aoyama & Reid 2006 both describe the dialect of Central Bontok spoken in barangay Guinaang, exactly the catalog's 'Central Bontok, Guinaang dialect'. Walrod 2006's Bontoc particle equivalents are labelled 'Central Bontoc' with no village given. The archive.org copy listed for Reid 1971 is the Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut) page, a different language.

There were exceptions for each criterion.' Verbatim. The only other 'stress' hit (p. 148) is Thurgood 1993's cross-linguistic claim about geminates after a short stressed vowel, not a Bontok rule. Appendix word list (pp. 155-156) marks acute on singleton-consonant words and shows both penultimate stress (ápo, ípit, aníto, kákak, ókip, óma, fáli, árang, kháwa, cháya, cháyon, káyang, isónga, nafáro, ílang, alíng) and final stress (kotó, kokó, esék, amó, amá, anák, iná, anáy, tongá, engér, langés, arók, s…
new_statements.relation_note: Implicit evidence only (marked forms in a word list, not a rule statement); agrees with Reid 2005 that stress is lexically variable (penult vs final) in Guinaang Bontok. Describes the Guinaang dialect specifically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is stated; the paper is an acoustic study of geminates. But the selection criterion 'had stress on the first syllable' (with exceptions) and the appendix word list, which marks disyllables with both penultimate stress (ápo 'grandfather', ípit 'squeeze', aníto 'ancestor spirit', kákak 'a bird', ókip 'pack', óma 'cut grass') and final stress (kotó 'head lice', kokó 'fingernail', esék 'seed', amó 'tame', amá 'father', anák 'child'), show that stress position varies from word to word in Guinaang Bontok, consistent with Reid 2005's 'contrastive stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: the authors note 'exceptions for each criterion', i.e. some analysed words were not initially stressed; stress is unmarked on the geminate-consonant forms in the appendix
new_statements.identity_note: Reid 2005 and Aoyama & Reid 2006 both describe the dialect of Central Bontok spoken in barangay Guinaang, exactly the catalog's 'Central Bontok, Guinaang dialect'. Walrod 2006's Bontoc particle equivalents are labelled 'Central Bontoc' with no village given. The archive.org copy listed for Reid 1971 is the Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut) page, a different language.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Reid 1963 PDF we hold/text at sec. 2 and sec. 2.1, pp. 2-3 of the revised copy, exactly as the locator says. (2) The source is a dedicated phonology article by the language's principal describer, based on two years of monolingual-village fieldwork, and its stress analysis (phonemic primary stress, unpredictable but within the last three syllables; length on stressed open penult/antepenult; predictable secondary stress) is restated unchanged in Reid 1976 (held), Reid 2005 (downloaded now, confirms 'contrastive stress' in both the 1960 and 2004 phonemic systems), Reid 2007/2011 (held) and the Minpaku Talking Dictionary (held). (3) Glottolog's longer 'grammars' are a 1909 pre-phonemic grammar that Reid 2007 explicitly faults on accent/length, a 1932 study, and a 1970 discourse grammar; web search found no later stress/prosody or acoustic-stress study

sources.citation: Walrod, Michael R. (2006). The marker is the message: the influence of discourse markers and particles on textual meaning.
sources.note: A discourse-particles paper, primarily on Ga'dang with Ilocano and Central Bontoc equivalents (Bontoc forms supplied by two speakers, fn. 5). The only prosody talk is 'semantic prosody' and a remark that Ga'dang interjections each carry 'a particular phonological prosody' (p. 10); nothing on word stress in Bontok or any language. The listed open_url is a landing page; the linked PDF path on sil.org 404s (redirect capitalises 'Philippines'), but the lowercase www-01.sil.org path serves the file, saved as noted.

sources.quote: This paper analyzes reduplication patterns in Bontok. ... The claim is that in Bontok heavy syllable reduplication interacts with two phonological processes: gemination and metathesis. It is suggested that these processes occur because there is a constraint preventing glottal stops from being introduced into syllable codas. It is also argued that in reduplication, not just the segmental structure is copied, but the prosodic template as well.
sources.locator: abstract (OpenAlex record); full text pp. 135-148 not obtained
sources.note: Only other prosodic-phonology treatment of (Guinaang) Bontok located; may restate stress/length interaction with reduplication, but is built on Reid's data and unlikely to change the lexical/three-syllable-window coding.
